title: Celsus on temples, altars and images
source_text: Φέρε δὲ ἴδωμεν καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, ἐν οἷς ταῦτά φησι· στῶμεν δ᾿ ἐκεῖθεν· οὐκ ἀνέχονται νεὼς ὁρῶντες καὶ βωμοὺς καὶ ἀγάλματα. οὐδὲ γὰρ Σκύθαι τοῦτο οὐδὲ Λιβύων οἱ Νομάδες οὐδὲ Σῆρες οἱ ἄθεοι οὐδ᾿ ἄλλα ἔθνη τὰ δυσαγέστατα καὶ ἀνομώτατα. ὅτι δὲ καὶ Πέρσαι οὕτως νομίζουσιν. Ἡρόδοτε ἐν τοῖσδε ἱστορεῖ· „Πέρσας δὲ οἶδα νόμοισι τοῖσδε χρεωμένους, ἀγάλματα μὲν καὶ βωμοὺς καὶ ναοὺς οὐκ ἐν νόμῳ ποιευμένους ἱδρύεσθαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖσι ποιεῦσι μωρίην ἐπιφέρουσιν· ὡς μὲν ἐμοὶ δοκέει. διότι οὐκ ἀνθρωποφυέας ἐνόμισαν τοὺς θεοὺς καθάπερ οἱ Ἕλληνες εἶναι.“ καὶ μὴν καὶ Ἡράκλειτος ὧδέ πως ἀποφαίνεται· „καὶ τοῖς ἀγάλμασι τουτέοισιν εὔχονται, ὁκοῖον εἴ τις τοῖς δόμοισι λεσχηνεύοιτο, οὔ τι γινώσκων θεοὺς οὐδ᾿ ἥρωας. οἵτινές εἰσι.“ τί γοῦν σοφώτερον τοῦ Ἡρακλείτου ἡμᾶς διδάσκουσιν; ὁ μέν γε μάλα ἀποῤῥήτως ὑποσημαίνει ἠλίθιον τὸ „τοῖς ἀγάλμασιν“ εὔχεσθαι, ἐὰν μὴ γινώσκῃ τις „θεοὺς καὶ ἥρωας. οἵτινές εἰσιν.“ Ἡράκλειτος μὲν οὕτως· οἱ δὲ ἄντικρυς τὰ ἀγάλματα ἀτιμάζουσιν. εἰ μὲν ὅτι λίθος ἢ ξύλον ἢ χαλκὸς ἢ χρυσὸς. ὃν ὁ δεῖνα ἢ ὁ δεῖνα εἰργάσατο, οὐκ ἂν εἴη θεὸς. γελοία ἡ σοφία. τίς γὰρ καὶ ἄλλος εἰ μὴ πάντῃ νήπιος ταῦτα ἡγεῖται θεοὺς ἀλλὰ θεῶν ἀναθήματα καὶ ἀγάλματα; εἰ δ᾿ ὅτι μηδὲ θείας εἰκόνας ὑποληπτέον. ἄλλην γὰρ εἶναι θεοῦ μορφὴν. ὥσπερ καὶ Πέρσαις δοκεῖ· λελήθασιν αὐτοὶ σφᾶς αὐτοὺς ἐλέγχοντες, ὅταν φῶσιν ὅτι „ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησε τὸν ἄνθρωπον“ ἰδίαν „εἰκόνα“ τὸ δὲ εἶδος ὅμοιον ἑαυτῷ. ἀλλὰ συνθήσονται μὲν εἶναι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τιμῇ τινων, ἢ ὁμοίων ἢ ἀνομοίων τὸ εἶδος, οὔτε δὲ θεοὺς εἶναι, οἷς ταῦτα ἀνάκειται, ἀλλὰ δαίμονας, οὐδὲ χρῆναι θεραπεύειν δαίμονας ὅστις σέβει θεόν.
pass_a_gloss: Come, let us see also the following, in which he says these: [Celsus:] Let us stand (ἵστημι) from there. They do not endure (ἀνέχομαι) seeing temples (νεῴς), altars (βωμοί) and images (ἀγάλματα). For not even [do] Scythians this, nor the Nomads of the Libyans, nor the Seres the godless (ἄθεοι), nor other nations (ἔθνη) most unholy (δυσαγέστατα) and most lawless (ἀνομώτατα). That the Persians also hold (νομίζω) so, Herodotus relates (ἱστορέω) in these: 'I know the Persians using these customs (νόμοι): images and altars and temples they do not hold it in custom to set up (ἱδρύω), but even to those making them they impute folly (μωρίη); as it seems to me, because they did not think the gods of human nature (ἀνθρωποφυέες) as the Greeks.' And indeed Heraclitus declares (ἀποφαίνομαι) somehow thus: 'And to these images they pray (εὔχομαι), as if one should chat (λεσχηνεύομαι) with houses (δόμοι), not knowing (γινώσκω) gods or heroes, who they are.' What then wiser than Heraclitus do they teach us? He at least very secretly (ἀπορρήτως) hints (ὑποσημαίνω) that foolish (ἠλίθιος) is praying 'to the images' if one does not know 'gods and heroes, who they are.' Heraclitus thus; but these outright (ἄντικρυς) dishonour (ἀτιμάζω) the images. If because stone or wood or bronze or gold, which so-and-so (ὁ δεῖνα) or so-and-so wrought (ἐργάζομαι), would not be a god, laughable (γελοία) the wisdom. For who else, if not wholly infant (νήπιος), considers these gods, rather than offerings (ἀναθήματα) and images of gods? But if because one must not even suppose (ὑπολαμβάνω) them divine likenesses (εἰκόνες), for God's form (μορφή) is other, as the Persians also think, they have escaped their own notice (λανθάνω) refuting (ἐλέγχω) themselves, when they say that 'God made man' his own 'image' (εἰκών) and the form (εἶδος) like himself. But they will agree (συντίθεμαι) that these are for the honour (τιμή) of certain ones, either like or unlike in form, but that those to whom these are dedicated (ἀνάκειμαι) are not gods but demons (δαίμονες), nor must whoever reveres (σέβω) God serve (θεραπεύω) demons.
pass_b_english: Come, let us look also at what follows, where he says this: “But let us stop there. They cannot bear the sight of temples and altars and images. Nor, for that matter, can the Scythians, nor the Nomads of Libya, nor the godless Seres, nor other nations, the most unholy and lawless. And that the Persians too hold this view, Herodotus records in these words: ‘I know that the Persians follow these customs: it is not their custom to set up images and altars and temples; rather, they even charge those who make them with folly, because, as it seems to me, they did not think, as the Greeks do, that the gods are of human nature’ (Herodotus, Histories 1.131). And indeed Heraclitus too declares something like this: ‘And they pray to these images, as if one were to chat with houses, knowing nothing of gods or heroes, who they are’ (Heraclitus, fragment 5 Diels-Kranz).

“What wiser thing, then, do they teach us than Heraclitus? He at any rate hints, in a deeply veiled way, that it is foolish to pray ‘to the images’ if one does not know ‘gods and heroes, who they are’. So much for Heraclitus; but these men openly dishonour the images. If it is because stone or wood or bronze or gold, which this man or that has made, could not be a god, their wisdom is ridiculous. For who else, unless he is a complete child, thinks these things are gods, and not offerings to the gods and images of them? But if it is because one must not even suppose them to be divine likenesses, since the form of God is different, as the Persians also think, then they do not notice that they refute themselves when they say that ‘God made man’ his own ‘image’ (Genesis 1:26–27), and his form like himself. They will agree, indeed, that these things exist in honour of certain beings, whether like them or unlike them in form; but they will say that those to whom they are dedicated are not gods but demons, and that whoever reveres God must not serve demons.”

choices.choice: The whole chapter is Celsus’s text; Origen’s answer begins in 7.63. στῶμεν δ᾿ ἐκεῖθεν is doubtful: taken as ‘let us stop there’, closing the previous topic; it could also mean ‘let us take our stand from there’. οὐδὲ γὰρ Σκύθαι τοῦτο: ‘nor [do] the Scythians [bear] this’, as Origen’s restatement in 7.63 confirms; γάρ rendered ‘for that matter’. Σῆρες: the Seres, a people of the far East (usually taken as the Chinese). Ἡρόδοτε in the staged text is a typo for Ἡρόδοτος. Herodotus, Histories 1.131 is quoted in Ionic. Heraclitus fragment 5 Diels-Kranz (also quoted at Contra Celsum 1.5). ὁ δεῖνα ἢ ὁ δεῖνα: ‘this man or that’. ‘God made man his own image, and his form like himself’ is Celsus’s paraphrase of Genesis 1:26–27, set in quotation marks only where his words echo the verse. δαίμονες rendered ‘demons’ because Celsus is reporting what Christians will say. The μέν ... δέ after συνθήσονται is rendered ‘They will agree ... but they will say’.
οὐδὲ γὰρ Σκύθαι: 'Nor indeed' -> 'Nor, for that matter,' (keeps γάρ); ἄλλα ἔθνη τὰ δυσαγέστατα: article kept, 'other nations, the most unholy and lawless'
ἄντικρυς ἀτιμάζουσιν: 'treat with open contempt' -> 'openly dishonour'
εἰργάσατο: archaic 'has wrought' -> 'has made'; γελοία ἡ σοφία: 'it is a ridiculous wisdom' -> 'their wisdom is ridiculous'
opening quotation mark added at the start of the second paragraph, since Celsus's quotation continues
Herodotus 1.131, Heraclitus fragment 5 DK and Genesis 1:26–27 checked
